lead: ADAS is a stack of sensors, perception, fusion, planning and actuation that warns the driver or takes over braking, steering or speed control. It exists because a machine can sense some hazards earlier than a tired driver, but it must work at a defined level of automation. You meet it in automatic emergency braking, lane keeping, blind spot warning, adaptive cruise and parking assist. This chapter is tagged advanced; only a few universities teach ADAS as a full chapter.
prereq: You need 5.2 for adaptive cruise, 5.3 for steering angle, and 5.7 for passive safety as the last resort.

sections.h3: The five-layer stack and SAE levels

blocks.text: ADAS is not one box. Sensors give raw data. Perception turns pixels and echoes into objects, lanes and signs. Fusion combines the sensors. Planning chooses a path and speed. Actuation commands brakes, steering and throttle. Figure 5.8.1 draws the chain from sensors on the left to actuation on the right, with the stopping distance of the worked example below it.

SAE levels run from 0 to 5. Level 0 has no automation. Level 1 assists one task, such as adaptive cruise. Level 2 handles steering and speed together, but the driver still monitors the road and remains responsible. Level 3 is conditional, Level 4 is high and Level 5 is full automation. Most ADAS here is Level 1 or 2.

A warning only alerts. An intervening function moves a control. Lane departure warning alerts; lane keep steers. The same stack serves both warning and action. The layers matter more than the brand names.

Every sensor is a trade-off. Camera: detail, low cost, weak in glare and fog. Radar: range and speed in bad weather, poor shape. Lidar: 3D cloud, higher cost, weak in dust. Ultrasonic: short range, cheap, good for parking.

Fusion combines them because one weakness is another strength. A camera sees lane lines that radar cannot; radar keeps measuring range and closing speed in rain, fog and low sun that blind a camera, while the camera can tell a stopped car from a bridge or sign that radar sees only as a stationary echo. Fusion needs time alignment and one vehicle coordinate frame.

Common functions: AEB brakes for a collision; lane departure warning alerts; lane keep steers; blind spot detection watches the side; adaptive cruise holds a gap (see adaptive cruise control); traffic sign recognition reads signs; parking assist uses ultrasonics; driver monitoring watches eyes and head. AEB, lane keep, adaptive cruise and parking assist act on the brakes, steering or throttle; lane departure warning, blind spot detection and traffic sign recognition mostly warn, though some blind spot systems also brake or steer. Driver monitoring is becoming common in Indian cars with camera-based attention checks.

sections.h3: AEB, delay and the safety limit

blocks.text: AEB shows the chain. Perception finds the object and estimates range and closing speed. Planning decides a crash is likely. Actuation builds brake pressure. Time passes in sensing, decision and brake build, so AEB cannot beat physics.
s is stopping distance (m), v is speed (m/s), t<sub>d</sub> is delay (s), a is braking deceleration (m/s²).

A quicker measure is time-to-collision, TTC = d ÷ v<sub>rel</sub>, the gap divided by the closing speed; AEB warns first and then brakes as TTC falls. At low speed AEB can stop the car. At high speed it may only reduce impact speed. The numbers decide the limit, not a fixed claim. The driver must still steer and brake in a Level 2 car.

A warning-only system does not brake; an intervening system does. Passive safety, such as the airbag, is the last resort after AEB fails. Functional safety asks what happens if a sensor is wrong or a brake command is late; ISO 26262 functional safety answers it formally. Fusion reduces false alarms and missed stops.

examples.question: A car at 50 km/h (use v = 13.9 m/s) approaches a stopped car. The AEB delay from first detection to full braking is 0.5 s, then braking is 8 m/s². Find the delay distance, braking distance and total distance; the TTC and the margin when the stopped car is first detected at 25 m, 30 m and 18 m; and the impact speed in the 18 m case.
steps: TTC at 25 m = 25 ÷ 13.9 = 1.80 s (2.16 s at 30 m, 1.29 s at 18 m). A stop is possible from 25 m and 30 m; from 18 m it is not.
Impact speed from 18 m: braking starts after 6.95 m, so it has 18 − 6.95 = 11.05 m. v² = 13.9² − 2 × 8 × 11.05 = 193.21 − 176.80 = 16.41, so v = 4.05 m/s (14.6 km/h), down from 50 km/h.
examples.answer: Delay 6.95 m, braking 12.08 m, total 19.03 m; margins 5.97 m (25 m), 10.97 m (30 m) and −1.03 m (18 m), so only the first two allow a stop; from 18 m the car still hits at 4.05 m/s (14.6 km/h).
examples.check:
v = 13.9
t_d = 0.5
a = 8.0
d_delay = v * t_d
d_brake = v * v / (2 * a)
d_total = d_delay + d_brake
print(round(d_delay, 2))
print(round(d_brake, 2))
print(round(d_total, 2))
print(round(25 - d_total, 2))
print(round(30 - d_total, 2))
print(round(18 - d_total, 2))
print(round(25/13.9,2), round(30/13.9,2), round(18/13.9,2), round((13.9**2-2*8*(18-6.95))**0.5,2))

traps: Level 2 is not self-driving; the driver still monitors the road and remains responsible.
Lane departure warning alerts; lane keep steers. A warning is not an intervention.
Convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6. Using km/h in place of m/s makes the delay term v t<sub>d</sub> 3.6 times too large and the braking term v²/(2a) 3.6² ≈ 13 times too large.
Delay distance is v t<sub>d</sub>, not v²/(2a). Do not count the delay twice.
A negative margin means the crash is unavoidable, not that the brakes failed.

quiz.a: Partial automation: the system steers and controls speed together, but the driver monitors the road all the time and remains responsible.

The camera gives detail (lanes, signs, object type) but is weak in glare and fog; radar measures range and closing speed in bad weather but sees shape poorly. Together they cover each other's weaknesses and cut false alarms and missed objects.

quiz.q: A car at 72 km/h has 0.4 s delay. Find delay distance.
Why can AEB not stop from 18 m if it needs 19.03 m?
quiz.a: The car needs 19.03 m but has 18 m, so 1.03 m is missing. It can only cut the impact speed, here to 4.05 m/s (14.6 km/h).

quiz.q: How does lane departure warning (LDW) differ from lane keeping assist (LKA)?
quiz.a: LDW only warns the driver, by a sound, a lamp or a seat or wheel vibration, when the car drifts over a line. LKA also steers, through the EPS motor, to bring the car back into the lane.

quiz.q: Which sensor do most parking-assist systems use, and why?
quiz.a: Ultrasonic sensors in the bumpers: they are cheap and measure short distances, up to a few metres, accurately at walking speed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry is moving ADAS into central domain controllers that fuse camera, radar and lidar on one board. Newer curricula add SOTIF, the safety of the intended function, and driver-monitoring rules. Search next for 'ADAS sensor fusion', 'AEB stopping distance' and 'ISO 26262'.
